scenes.title: The Myrmidons Mourn Patroclus
scenes.summary: The Achaeans scatter to their ships, but Achilles keeps the Myrmidons in their chariots: three times they drive around the body of Patroclus, weeping, and Thetis rouses in them the longing for lament. Laying his man-slaying hands on his companion's breast, Achilles tells him that he is fulfilling all that he promised, to give Hector raw to the dogs and to cut the throats of twelve Trojan children before his pyre, and he stretches Hector face down in the dust beside the bier. Then he gives the Myrmidons a funeral feast, and the blood of oxen, sheep, goats and hogs runs all around the body.

scenes.title: Achilles Refuses to Wash
scenes.summary: The kings bring Achilles to Agamemnon's hut and have the heralds set a tripod over the fire, hoping to persuade him to wash off the clotted blood, but he swears by Zeus that no water will come near his head until he has laid Patroclus on the fire, heaped up a mound and cut his hair. He bids Agamemnon send for wood at dawn, and they yield to the hateful feast. Afterward Achilles lies groaning on the shore of the loud-roaring sea among the Myrmidons.

scenes.title: The Ghost of Patroclus
scenes.summary: As Achilles sleeps, the soul of Patroclus comes to him, like him in all things, and asks to be buried quickly, for the souls of the dead will not let him cross the river into the house of Hades. Achilles too is fated to die beneath the wall of Troy; let their bones lie together in one urn, the golden two-handled jar that Thetis gave, as they were reared together in Peleus' house after Menoetius brought him from Opus, a boy who had killed the son of Amphidamas in anger over knucklebones. Achilles promises, and reaches out to embrace him, but the soul goes beneath the earth like smoke, gibbering. Achilles springs up: even in the house of Hades there is a soul and a phantom, but no mind in it at all.

scenes.title: The Wood and the Hair
scenes.summary: At dawn Agamemnon sends mules and men under Meriones to cut oaks on the slopes of Ida, and they throw the logs down on the shore where Achilles has planned a great barrow for Patroclus and for himself. The Myrmidons arm and carry the body out in procession, covering it with the hair they cut off, while Achilles holds the head. Achilles cuts the hair that he had grown long for the river Spercheius, as his father vowed for his homecoming, and, since he will not go home, places it in the hands of Patroclus.

scenes.title: The Pyre
scenes.summary: At Achilles' word Agamemnon dismisses the army to supper, and those who cared for the dead build a pyre a hundred feet each way and lay the body on top. Achilles covers it with the fat of flayed sheep and cattle, sets jars of honey and ointment against the bier, and throws on the pyre four horses, two of his nine dogs, and twelve sons of the Trojans, cut down with the bronze; Hector, he tells Patroclus, he will give to the dogs, not to the fire. But Aphrodite keeps the dogs from Hector day and night and anoints him with ambrosial oil, and Apollo covers the place with a dark cloud, so that the sun does not parch his skin.

scenes.title: The Winds
scenes.summary: The pyre will not burn. Achilles prays to the North Wind and the West Wind, promising fine sacrifices, and Iris finds the winds feasting in the house of the West Wind; she will not sit, for she is going to the hecatombs of the Ethiopians, and gives them Achilles' prayer. The winds rush over the sea and fall on the pyre, and all night long they toss its flame, while Achilles pours wine on the ground, calling on the soul of Patroclus, and mourns as a father mourns who burns the bones of his son, newly married.

scenes.title: The Bones and the Mound
scenes.summary: When the morning star rises the pyre dies down, and the winds go home over the Thracian sea. Achilles sleeps a little, until the leaders come and wake him; he bids them quench the pyre with wine and gather the bones of Patroclus, which lie apart in the middle of the pyre, into a golden bowl, in a double fold of fat, until he himself is hidden in Hades. The tomb is to be no greater than is fitting; the Achaeans who outlive him are to make it wide and high. They gather the bones, mark out the circle of the mound, and heap up the earth.

scenes.title: The Prizes and the Entrants
scenes.summary: Achilles keeps the army in a wide gathering and brings prizes out of the ships. For the chariot race he sets a woman skilled in flawless handiwork and a tripod with handles, a mare carrying a mule foal, a cauldron, two talents of gold and a two-handled bowl. He himself will not race: his immortal horses, Poseidon's gift to Peleus, stand mourning their kind charioteer. Eumelus, son of Admetus, rises first, then Diomedes with the horses of Tros that he took from Aeneas, Menelaus with his own Podargus and Agamemnon's mare Aethe, given by Echepolus so that he need not go to Ilios, and Antilochus with horses born in Pylos.

scenes.title: Nestor's Advice
scenes.summary: Nestor tells Antilochus that his horses are the slowest, and that a charioteer wins by cunning more than by strength, as a woodcutter or a helmsman does. He describes the turning post, a dry stump of oak or pine with two white stones leaning against it, perhaps the mound of a man who died long ago, and tells him to drive close to it, leaning to the left and goading on the right-hand horse, and to let the hub seem to graze it without touching the stone. Meriones makes ready fifth; Achilles shakes the lots, and sets Phoenix by the turning post as a lookout.

scenes.title: The Chariot Race
scenes.summary: The chariots cross the plain. On the stretch back Eumelus' mares lead, with Diomedes' horses close behind, when Apollo knocks the whip from Diomedes' hand; Athena gives it back, puts might into his horses, and breaks Eumelus' yoke, and he is thrown from the chariot. Antilochus warns his father's horses not to let Aethe, a mare, shame them, or Nestor will kill them, and where winter water has broken the road he drives beside Menelaus; Menelaus holds back to avoid a crash and calls him the most baneful of mortals, who will not have the prize without an oath.

scenes.title: Idomeneus and Ajax Quarrel
scenes.summary: From his lookout Idomeneus makes out a horse in the lead, bay with a white mark on its forehead, and thinks the driver is Diomedes. Ajax, son of Oileus, tells him that he blusters and that his eyes are not the sharpest: Eumelus' mares are leading still. Idomeneus offers to wager a tripod or a cauldron, with Agamemnon as arbiter, and Ajax rises to answer him, until Achilles bids them stop and watch.

scenes.title: The Finish
scenes.summary: Diomedes drives in, his horses streaming sweat, and Sthenelus takes the woman and the tripod. Antilochus comes in second, by crafty ways, with Menelaus close behind; then Meriones, and last Eumelus, dragging his chariot. Achilles pities him and proposes to give him the second prize, but Antilochus rises to claim the mare and dares any man to fight him for her; Achilles smiles, and gives Eumelus the corselet he took from Asteropaeus.

scenes.title: Menelaus and Antilochus
scenes.summary: Menelaus takes the scepter and accuses Antilochus of shaming his prowess by throwing worse horses in front of his; he asks the leaders to judge between them impartially, and then, so that no Achaean may say he overpowered Antilochus with lies, proposes a judgment of his own: Antilochus must stand before his horses, whip in hand, and swear by Poseidon that he did not hamper his chariot by a trick. Antilochus yields, pleading his youth, and gives up the mare. Menelaus' heart is warmed, as when there is dew around the ears of a growing crop; for the sake of all that Antilochus and his father and brother have suffered for him he gives her back, and takes the cauldron.

scenes.title: Nestor's Prize
scenes.summary: Meriones takes the two talents, and the fifth prize, the two-handled bowl, is left over; Achilles gives it to Nestor as a memorial of the funeral of Patroclus, since grievous old age keeps him from the contests. Nestor accepts and remembers the funeral games of Amarynceus at Buprasium, where he won at boxing, wrestling, running and the spear, and was beaten only in the chariot race by the twin sons of Actor.

scenes.title: The Boxing
scenes.summary: For the boxing Achilles sets out a hard-working mule and a two-handled cup. Epeius, son of Panopeus, lays hold of the mule and boasts that, though he falls short in battle, no one will beat him at boxing; only Euryalus, son of Mecisteus, stands up against him, with Diomedes to gird him and cheer him on. Epeius strikes him on the cheek, and he leaps up like a fish in the ripple of the North Wind and falls; Epeius sets him on his feet, and his companions lead him away, spitting thick blood.

scenes.title: The Wrestling
scenes.summary: For the wrestling the prizes are a great tripod valued at twelve oxen and a woman skilled in many works valued at four. Telamonian Ajax and Odysseus grapple like the rafters of a high house, and neither can throw the other, until Ajax lifts Odysseus, and Odysseus strikes the hollow of his knee and falls on top of him; at the second attempt both fall together. Achilles stops them: victory is for both, and they are to take equal prizes.

scenes.title: The Footrace
scenes.summary: The first prize for the footrace is a silver mixing bowl made by the Sidonians, which Euneus, son of Jason, gave Patroclus as the price of Lycaon; then an ox, and half a talent of gold. Ajax, son of Oileus, leads, with Odysseus as close behind him as the rod to a weaving woman's breast; Odysseus prays to Athena, and Ajax slips in the dung of the slain oxen and comes in second, complaining that the goddess stands by Odysseus like a mother. Antilochus, last, says that the gods honor older men and praises Achilles, who adds half a talent to his prize.

scenes.title: The Armed Duel
scenes.summary: Achilles sets out the spear, shield and helmet of Sarpedon, which Patroclus took from him, and bids two men put on their armor and fight until one draws blood. Telamonian Ajax and Diomedes come together three times; Ajax's spear is stopped by the corselet, and Diomedes keeps reaching for his neck over the great shield, until the Achaeans, fearing for Ajax, make them stop and take equal prizes; Achilles gives Diomedes the sword.

scenes.title: The Weight Throw
scenes.summary: Achilles sets out a lump of rough-cast iron that Eetion used to hurl before Achilles killed him: the winner will have iron for five years. Epeius throws first, and the Achaeans laugh; Leonteus and Telamonian Ajax throw farther, but Polypoetes throws beyond them all, as far as a herdsman's throwing stick flies over the herd.

scenes.title: The Archery and the Javelin
scenes.summary: For the archers Achilles sets ten double axes and ten single axes, and ties a dove by a cord to the mast of a ship. Teucer, who makes no vow to Apollo, misses the bird and cuts the cord; Meriones vows a hecatomb to Apollo and shoots the dove as she circles under the clouds. For the javelin Agamemnon and Meriones stand up, but Achilles gives Agamemnon the cauldron without a contest, as the best of all, and the spear to Meriones; Agamemnon gives his prize to the herald Talthybius.

days.label: Day 27
days.note: The evening of the fourth day of battle: the Myrmidons mourn Patroclus and feast beside his bier, and the kings bring Achilles to Agamemnon's hut, where he refuses to wash and bids Agamemnon send for wood at dawn (23.49–50).

days.label: Night of Day 27
days.note: The night after the fourth day of battle: the soul of Patroclus comes to Achilles as he sleeps on the shore, and stands over him “all night long” (23.105); the Myrmidons weep until dawn.

days.label: Day 28
days.note: Rosy-fingered Dawn appears to the mourners (23.109): wood is brought from Ida, Patroclus is carried out and laid on the pyre with the sacrifices, and the North and West Winds come at Achilles' prayer to kindle it.

days.label: Night of Day 28
days.note: The winds toss the flame of the pyre “all night long”, and all night long Achilles pours wine on the ground, calling on the soul of Patroclus (23.217–221).

days.label: Day 29
days.note: At the rising of the morning star the pyre dies down (23.226–228); the bones are gathered, the mound is heaped up, and Achilles holds the funeral games. The day ends at the beginning of Book 24, when the gathering breaks up and the army goes to supper and sleep (24.1–3).
